description: Roman women who wielded real power — Livia, Agrippina the Younger, and the Egyptian queen Cleopatra VII.
content_html:
Power behind the Throne

The Roman imperial system, which replaced the Republic in 27 BC, created new possibilities for powerful women. An emperor’s wife, mother, or sister lived at the heart of power, had daily access to the most important man in the world, and could influence appointments, policies, and the fate of rivals. The Roman Senate remained exclusively male, but the imperial household was not governed by the same formal rules, and women who knew how to operate within it could be genuinely formidable. Ancient sources — almost all male, almost all hostile — were simultaneously fascinated and alarmed by these women, producing portraits that blend genuine observation with exaggeration and moral condemnation.

Livia: The Perfect Empress

Livia Drusilla was the wife of Rome’s first emperor, Augustus, whom she married in 38 BC. She remained his wife until his death in AD 14 — a period of over fifty years. During the Augustan age she became a public symbol of Roman wifely virtue: chaste, dignified, devoted to her husband and household. Augustus, who was promoting a moral reform programme for Rome, projected Livia as the model Roman matrona. She was depicted in sculpture as serene and modest. The Ara Pacis (Altar of Peace), a great carved marble monument commissioned by the Senate in 13 BC to celebrate Augustus’s return from campaigns in Spain and Gaul, shows Livia in the sacrificial procession alongside Augustus, her children, and senior figures of the state. She is depicted veiled (a sign of ritual purity) and takes her place as a central figure in the Augustan dynasty’s self-presentation.

Yet Livia’s influence went far beyond the ceremonial. Ancient sources, including the historian Tacitus and the biographer Suetonius, hint that she managed significant patronage networks, interceded with Augustus on behalf of petitioners, and exerted influence over matters of succession. After Augustus’s death she received unprecedented honours: the Senate granted her the title “Julia Augusta” and she was eventually deified (made a goddess) under the emperor Claudius in AD 42. The Laudatio Turiae, a Roman funerary inscription (probably dating to the late first century BC and perhaps connected to the civil-war period), praises a Roman wife in similar terms to Livia — loyalty, endurance, and selfless support for her husband — suggesting that Livia represented one ideal end of a spectrum of Roman female virtue that was genuinely valued, not simply invented for propaganda.

Key Fact

Livia, wife of Augustus, was presented as the model Roman matrona: chaste, dignified and devoted. The Ara Pacis depicts her in the dynastic procession, veiled as a sign of purity. After Augustus’s death she was granted the title “Julia Augusta” and was eventually deified under Claudius.

Agrippina the Younger: Power and Danger

Agrippina the Younger represents a more alarming figure in Roman historical memory. As the mother of the emperor Nero and wife of the emperor Claudius, she occupied a uniquely powerful position in mid-first century AD Rome. The historian Tacitus, in his Annals, portrays her as relentlessly ambitious — pursuing power through a series of strategic marriages, allegedly poisoning her husband Claudius to secure Nero’s succession, and then attempting to dominate her son’s reign. Tacitus describes her appearing in public seated on a dais alongside Nero at official ceremonies, receiving foreign ambassadors, and being acclaimed on coins alongside the emperor as a co-regent figure.

Roman coins from the early years of Nero’s reign (AD 54–55) show Agrippina’s head on the obverse (front) of the coin alongside her son, or even placed in front of his head, implying her precedence. This is a material source of great significance: official state coinage is one of the most authoritative forms of public communication in the Roman world, and depicting a woman in this position is extraordinary. Nero eventually had his mother murdered in AD 59, and after her death the hostile portrait in the literary sources hardened. Tacitus’s account must be read sceptically, since it was written well after the events and draws on hostile senatorial tradition.

The portraits of Livia and Agrippina in sources such as Tacitus and Suetonius are deeply shaped by senatorial ideology: powerful women who operated beyond their proper sphere were inherently suspect. Livia is praised where she conformed to the matrona ideal; Agrippina is condemned for the same ambition that would have been admired in a male politician. The material sources — coins showing Agrippina and Nero; the Ara Pacis showing Livia in the dynastic procession — cannot lie in the same way as literary texts, since they were produced for public display. But they too were constructed images: the Ara Pacis was official Augustan propaganda, not a neutral record. Using both literary and material sources together, and asking what each was designed to communicate, gives a more complete picture than either alone.

Cleopatra VII: Rome’s Most Feared Foreign Queen

Cleopatra VII was not a Roman woman, but Rome’s obsession with her makes her essential for this topic. As queen of Egypt she was an independent sovereign ruler with a large army, great wealth, and strategic control of Egypt’s grain supply, on which Rome depended. She forged a political and personal alliance with Julius Caesar after his arrival in Egypt in 48 BC, and later with his successor Mark Antony. The Roman poet Horace, writing after her defeat, calls her a deadly monster who corrupted Roman men with her un-Roman luxury and ambition. Virgil’s Aeneid (Book 8, lines 671–713) depicts the battle of Actium (31 BC) on the shield of Aeneas, where Cleopatra appears as a shameful eastern queen surrounded by monster-gods, opposed by the orderly Roman gods championing Octavian.

In 31 BC Octavian (later Augustus) defeated the combined forces of Antony and Cleopatra at the naval battle of Actium, off the western coast of Greece. Both Antony and Cleopatra subsequently took their own lives, and Egypt became a Roman province. The official Roman interpretation of the war was not a civil conflict between Roman generals, but a war against a foreign queen who had bewitched a Roman man and threatened to move the capital of the world from Rome to Alexandria. By framing Cleopatra as a foreign threat, Octavian could present his victory as the defence of Rome against an alien, feminised East — a narrative that shaped how Cleopatra was remembered for centuries.

Key Fact

Cleopatra was presented in Roman sources as a dangerous foreign queen who had seduced Roman generals away from their Roman values. Virgil’s Aeneid and Horace’s poetry treat her as a moral threat; the shield of Aeneas in Aeneid Book 8 depicts the battle of Actium with Cleopatra on the side of monstrous foreign gods. Her defeat in 31 BC allowed Octavian to present himself as the saviour of Roman tradition.

There is a recurring pattern in how Roman culture handled powerful women: it idealised women who exercised power invisibly (Livia as the perfect wife behind the scenes), feared women who sought visible political power (Agrippina appearing in public as co-ruler), and demonised foreign women who wielded power on their own terms (Cleopatra as eastern monster-queen). Each figure is a mirror held up to Roman anxieties about gender, power, and what it meant to be Roman. The material sources — the Ara Pacis, the coins of Agrippina, the funerary stele tradition across both cultures — remind us that behind the literary constructions were real women whose lives shaped the course of ancient history.
exam_tip_html: In essays about Roman women and power, always distinguish between the three figures: Livia (praised for operating through her husband), Agrippina (condemned for seeking visible power), and Cleopatra (demonised as a foreign threat). Each represents a different Roman response to the same underlying anxiety. When analysing the Ara Pacis or Nero’s coins as material sources, ask: what was this object designed to communicate, and for what audience? Official state art is propaganda, not neutral evidence, but it is still valuable precisely because it shows what powerful people wanted to project. Do not confuse Agrippina the Younger with Agrippina the Elder — examiners notice this distinction.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Imperial Roman women such as Livia and Agrippina the Younger exercised real political influence through proximity to the emperor, but Roman sources judged them by whether they conformed to the ideal of the invisible, modest matrona (Livia praised) or overstepped it (Agrippina condemned).
  • Cleopatra VII was not Roman but was the most feared woman in Roman political memory: Roman sources (Virgil, Horace) depicted her as a dangerous foreign queen who corrupted Roman men; Octavian’s victory at Actium was presented as Rome defeating an alien, feminised threat.
  • Material sources (the Ara Pacis, Nero’s coins with Agrippina) provide evidence for powerful women that cannot be dismissed as literary bias, but they too were constructed for political purposes and must be read as propaganda as well as evidence.

practice_questions.text: Name the Roman monument that depicts Livia in the dynastic procession alongside Augustus.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: the Ara Pacis (Altar of Peace). Accept 'the Ara Pacis Augustae'.

practice_questions.text: Describe how Agrippina the Younger is depicted on coins from the early years of Nero's reign.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for any three of: her head appears on the obverse (front) of the coin; she is shown alongside Nero's head; on some issues her portrait is placed in front of Nero's, implying precedence; coins are official state coinage, suggesting her co-ruler status was at least briefly acknowledged; this is extraordinary because women were not normally depicted on imperial coinage in this dominant way.

practice_questions.text:
Read the following passage, which paraphrases Virgil's Aeneid Book 8 (lines 671–713) describing the shield of Aeneas at the battle of Actium:

'On one side, Augustus stands at the bow with the Senate and people behind him, and the gods of Rome — including Apollo — fight for him. On the other side stands Antony, with his foreign armies and the wealth of the east, and beside him the Egyptian queen, facing the Roman gods with her own monstrous deities: jackal-headed Anubis barking against Neptune and Minerva. The queen signals her fleet with a golden rattle.'

What does this passage reveal about how Romans viewed Cleopatra? Use specific details from the passage.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A detailed analysis using multiple specific details from the passage (Cleopatra aligned with monstrous foreign gods against the orderly Roman gods; the golden rattle is a detail of decadence and foreignness; she is contrasted with Augustus's Roman Senate and people; Antony has been absorbed into the foreign, feminised East). Connects these details to the broader Roman cultural construction of Cleopatra as a threat to Roman values and uses Virgil’s Aeneid as official Augustan propaganda that served Octavian's post-Actium narrative. Reaches a supported judgement about what this reveals: Roman anxiety about powerful foreign women, the feminisation of the enemy, and the use of the epic genre for political purposes.
Secure: Uses at least two specific details and explains what they reveal about Roman attitudes to Cleopatra. Makes a clear point about the source as propaganda rather than neutral record.
Developing: Identifies one or two details and makes a basic observation, but the analysis of significance is limited or undeveloped.
Emerging: Paraphrases the passage or makes only very general observations.

practice_questions.text: Explain how the Ara Pacis is useful as evidence for Livia's position in Augustan Rome.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying what the Ara Pacis is (a carved marble monument commissioned by the Senate in 13 BC to celebrate Augustus). 1 mark for describing Livia's depiction (she appears in the sacrificial procession, veiled as a sign of ritual purity, alongside Augustus). 1 mark for explaining what this reveals (she was a central, public figure in the Augustan dynasty's self-presentation, not merely a private wife). 1 mark for a critical point (the Ara Pacis is official propaganda; it shows what Augustus wanted Rome to see, not necessarily Livia's actual influence; or, the fact that she appears in official state art at all is remarkable given that Roman women were normally confined to the domestic sphere).

practice_questions.text: How far does the evidence suggest that Roman imperial women were genuinely powerful, rather than simply used as symbols? Use named sources in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A well-structured argument distinguishing between symbolic power (Livia as model matrona on the Ara Pacis; Cleopatra as the constructed enemy of Augustan propaganda) and real political influence (Livia's patronage networks and role in succession politics; Agrippina's public appearances as apparent co-ruler, evidenced by Tacitus and the coins; Cleopatra's genuine military and economic power as an independent ruler). Uses named sources for both literary and material evidence. Critically addresses the reliability of Tacitus's hostile portraits. Reaches a supported judgement: some imperial women had real power; all were simultaneously used as symbols, and the two are not mutually exclusive.
Secure: Covers both symbolic and real aspects of imperial women's power with named evidence. Makes a clear argument and reaches a conclusion, even if source critique is limited.
Developing: Covers some relevant material but the argument is uneven; may focus mainly on one woman or not distinguish clearly between symbol and agent.
Emerging: Makes general points about powerful women without consistent use of named sources.

practice_questions.text: Compare how Roman literary sources and material sources portray powerful women differently. Use at least two examples of each type of source.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A clear comparison identifying that literary sources (Tacitus on Agrippina, Virgil and Horace on Cleopatra) tend to be moralistic, hostile, and shaped by cultural anxieties about women who exceeded their proper role; whereas material sources (Ara Pacis, Nero’s coins, funerary stelai) show women in official or commemorative contexts that can be analysed for what powerful people chose to project. Notes that both types are constructed: the Ara Pacis is Augustan propaganda; Tacitus reflects senatorial ideology. Reaches a supported conclusion about how combining both types gives a more nuanced picture.
Secure: Gives two examples of each type of source and identifies at least one meaningful difference in how they portray powerful women. Supports with named evidence.
Developing: Covers sources from mainly one type, or lists examples without comparing them meaningfully.
Emerging: Mentions sources without analysing how they differ in their portrayal.

knowledge_checks.q: The Ara Pacis is a carved marble monument that depicts Livia in a dynastic procession. When was it commissioned?
options: 31 BC, to celebrate the battle of Actium
13 BC, to celebrate Augustus's return from campaigns in Spain and Gaul
AD 14, to mark the death of Augustus
AD 42, when Livia was deified by Claudius

knowledge_checks.q: How does Virgil's Aeneid (Book 8) portray Cleopatra at the battle of Actium?
options: As a brave queen fighting for her country's independence
As a neutral observer of the battle
As a dangerous foreign queen aligned with monstrous eastern gods against Roman order
As a loyal ally of Augustus helping to defeat Mark Antony

knowledge_checks.q: Agrippina the Younger was the mother of the emperor _____ and is portrayed by Tacitus as attempting to dominate his early reign.
The _____ is an official Augustan propaganda monument that depicts Livia in the dynastic procession, veiled as a sign of ritual purity.
Match each powerful woman to the key evidence or source associated with her:
right: Ara Pacis — depicted veiled in the dynastic procession
Coins showing her portrait alongside (and sometimes in front of) Nero's
Virgil's Aeneid shows her opposing Roman gods at Actium

flashcard_questions.a: He wrote well after the events, drawing on hostile senatorial tradition that was biased against powerful women.
A Roman funerary inscription praising a wife for loyalty and self-sacrifice during the civil wars.

glossary_terms.definition: Wife of the emperor Augustus and mother of Tiberius; one of the most powerful women in Roman history, eventually deified under Claudius.
A respectable married Roman woman, the female counterpart of the male citizen, idealised for chastity, modesty, and management of the household.
Daughter of Germanicus and mother of Nero; portrayed in hostile ancient sources as dominating the early years of Nero's reign and attempting to co-rule Rome.
The last ruler of the Ptolemaic dynasty of Egypt, famous for her alliances with Julius Caesar and Mark Antony and the political threat she represented to Rome before her defeat at Actium in 31 BC.
An upright stone slab used as a grave marker, often carved with a relief scene; used in both Greek and Roman cultures to commemorate and memorialise the dead.
